title: What I've Learned from Users: why YC works and why founders misjudge their problems
summary: Graham reflects on what YC learned from advising many startups: most share the same problems, founders misjudge which matter most, and they resist advice because startups are counterintuitive. Speed defines startups, focus enables speed, and YC's value is improving focus and providing colleagues.

principles.text: Best application advice: explain what you've learned from users. It tests attention, understanding and how much they need your product.
principles.quote: Explain what you've learned from users.

principles.text: Founders often miss their biggest problem. Ask whether you'd use the product yourself if you hadn't built it.
principles.quote: Or founders will come in worried that they still haven't cracked the problem of user acquisition, and the reason turns out to be that their product isn't good enough.

principles.text: Prioritize ruthlessly: founders know their problems but not their relative importance, so find the one that will kill the company.
principles.quote: Often founders know what their problems are, but not their relative importance.

principles.text: Advice sounds wrong because startups are counterintuitive, so founders don't believe it until experience teaches them.
principles.quote: when you tell someone something counterintuitive, what it sounds to them is wrong. So the reason founders don't listen to us is that they don't believe us.

principles.text: Work in short cycles: find the key problem, try a fix, measure within a week. Be decisive at micro scale, tentative at macro scale.
principles.quote: If you correct course at a high enough frequency, you can be simultaneously decisive at a micro scale and tentative at a macro scale.

principles.text: Speed defines startups and focus enables it. Better navigation makes you faster twice over.
principles.quote: Speed defines startups. Focus enables speed. YC improves focus.
